Most LLM design output is bad because the model jumps to a default aesthetic instead of reading the room.\n    16\t\n    17\t### 0.A Read these signals first\n    18\t1. **Page kind** - landing (SaaS / consumer / agency / event), portfolio (dev / designer / creative studio), redesign (preserve vs overhaul), editorial / blog.\n    19\t2. **Vibe words** the user used - \"minimalist\", \"calm\", \"Linear-style\", \"Awwwards\", \"brutalist\", \"premium consumer\", \"Apple-y\", \"playful\", \"serious B2B\", \"editorial\", \"agency-y\", \"glassy\", \"dark tech\".\n    20\t3. **Reference signals** - URLs they linked, screenshots they pasted, products they named, brands they're competing with.\n    21\t4. **Audience** - B2B procurement panel vs. design-conscious consumer vs. recruiter scanning a portfolio. BRIEF \u2192 DESIGN SYSTEM MAP\n    83\t\n    84\tOnce you have the design read (Section 0) and dials (Section 1), pick the right foundation. DEFAULT ARCHITECTURE & CONVENTIONS\n   123\t\n   124\tUnless the design read picks a real design system (Section 2.A), these are the defaults:\n   125\t\n   126\t### 3.A Stack\n   127\t* **Framework:** React or Next.js. Default to Server Components (RSC).\n   128\t  * **RSC SAFETY:** Global state works ONLY in Client Components. In Next.js, wrap providers in a `\"use client\"` component.\n   129\t  * **INTERACTIVITY ISOLATION:** Any component using Motion, scroll listeners, or pointer physics MUST be an isolated leaf with `'use client'` at the top. Server Components render static layouts only.\n   130\t* **Styling:** **Tailwind v4** (default). Tailwind v3 only if the existing project demands it.\n   131\t  * For v4: do NOT use `tailwindcss` plugin in `postcss.config.js`. The `framer-motion` package still works as a legacy alias - prefer `motion/react` in new code.\n   133\t* **Fonts:** Always use `next/font` (Next.js) or self-host with `@font-face` + `font-display: swap`. Use Motion's `useMotionValue` / `useTransform` / `useScroll`. `useState` re-renders the React tree on every change and collapses on mobile.\n   139\t\n   140\t### 3.C Icons\n   141\t* **Allowed libraries (priority order):** `@phosphor-icons/react`, `hugeicons-react`, `@radix-ui/react-icons`, `@tabler/icons-react`.\n   142\t* **Discouraged:** `lucide-react`. Acceptable only when the user explicitly asks for it or the project already depends on it.\n   143\t* **NEVER hand-roll SVG icons.** If a glyph is missing, install a second library or compose from primitives - do not draw icon paths from scratch.\n   144\t* **One family per project.** Do not mix Phosphor with Lucide in the same component tree.\n   145\t* **Standardize `strokeWidth` globally** (e.g. `1.5` or `2.0`).\n   146\t\n   147\t### 3.D Emoji Policy\n   148\tDiscouraged by default in code, markup, and visible text. BRIEF INFERENCE (Read the Room Before Anything Else)\\n\\nBefore touching code or tweaking dials, **infer what the user actually wants**. Most LLM design output is bad because the model jumps to a default aesthetic instead of reading the room.\\n\\n### 0.A Read these signals first\\n1. **Page kind** - landing (SaaS / consumer / agency / event), portfolio (dev / designer / creative studio), redesign (preserve vs overhaul), editorial / blog.\\n2. **Vibe words** the user used - \\\"minimalist\\\", \\\"calm\\\", \\\"Linear-style\\\", \\\"Awwwards\\\", \\\"brutalist\\\", \\\"premium consumer\\\", \\\"Apple-y\\\", \\\"playful\\\", \\\"serious B2B\\\", \\\"editorial\\\", \\\"agency-y\\\", \\\"glassy\\\", \\\"dark tech\\\".\\n3. **Reference signals** - URLs they linked, screenshots they pasted, products they named, brands they're competing with.\\n4. **Audience** - B2B procurement panel vs. design-conscious consumer vs. recruiter scanning a portfolio. DESIGN ENGINEERING DIRECTIVES (Bias Correction)\n   162\t\n   163\tLLMs default to clich\u00e9s. Override these defaults proactively. Each rule has a context-aware override path.\n   164\t\n   165\t### 4.1 Typography\n   166\t* **Display / Headlines:** Default `text-4xl md:text-6xl tracking-tighter leading-none`.\n   167\t* **Body / Paragraphs:** Default `text-base text-gray-600 leading-relaxed max-w-[65ch]`.\n   168\t* **Sans font choice:**\n   169\t  * **Discouraged as default:** `Inter`. Pick `Geist`, `Outfit`, `Cabinet Grotesk`, `Satoshi`, or a brand-appropriate serif first.\n   170\t  * **Override:** Inter is acceptable when the user explicitly asks for a neutral / standard / Linear-style feel, or when the brief is a public-sector / accessibility-first site.\n   171\t* **Pairings to know:** `Geist` + `Geist Mono`, `Satoshi` + `JetBrains Mono`, `Cabinet Grotesk` + `Inter Tight`, `GT America` + `IBM Plex Mono`.\n   172\t\n   173\t* **SERIF DISCIPLINE (VERY DISCOURAGED AS DEFAULT):**\n   174\t  * Serif is **very discouraged as the default font for any project.** \"It feels creative / premium / editorial\" is NOT a reason to reach for serif. The agent's default mental model that \"creative brief = serif\" is the single most-tested AI tell in production rounds.\n   175\t  * **Serif is only acceptable when ONE of these is explicitly true:**\n   176\t    - The brand brief literally names a serif font, OR\n   177\t    - The aesthetic family is genuinely editorial / luxury / publication / manuscript / heritage / vintage AND you can articulate why this specific serif fits this specific brand\n   178\t  * For everything else (creative agency, design studio, modern brand, premium consumer, portfolio, lifestyle), **default sans-serif display** (Geist Display, ABC Diatype, S\u00f6hne Breit, Cabinet Grotesk Display, Migra Sans, GT Walsheim, Inter Display, PP Neue Montreal). Sans display fonts are not \"boring\" \u2014 they are the default for the same reason black is the default in fashion.\n   179\t  * **EMPHASIS RULE (related):** When you want to emphasize a word within a headline (the kinetic \"and `spatial` design\" type move), use **italic or bold of the SAME font**. Do NOT inject a random serif word into a sans headline (or vice versa) just to add visual interest. Mixed-family emphasis is amateur. Italic/bold emphasis in the same family is the right move.\n   180\t  * **Specifically BANNED as defaults:** `Fraunces` and `Instrument_Serif` (the two LLM-favorite display serifs).\n   181\t  * **If a serif is justified** (rare, per the above), rotate from this pool, do NOT reuse the same serif across consecutive projects: PP Editorial New, GT Sectra Display, Cardinal Grotesque, Reckless Neue, Tiempos Headline, Recoleta, Cormorant Garamond, Playfair Display, EB Garamond, IvyPresto, Migra, Editorial Old, Saol Display, S\u00f6hne Breit Kursiv, Domaine Display, Canela, Schnyder, Tobias, NB Architekt, ITC Galliard.\n   182\t\n   183\t* **ITALIC DESCENDER CLEARANCE (mandatory):** When italic is used in display type and the word contains a descender letter (`y g j p q`), `leading-[1]` or `leading-none` will clip the descender. Use `leading-[1.1]` minimum and add `pb-1` or `mb-1` reserve on the wrapping element. Audit every italic word in display headlines before shipping.\n   184\t\n   185\t### 4.2 Color Calibration\n   186\t* Max 1 accent color. Use neutral bases (Zinc / Slate / Stone) with high-contrast singular accents (Emerald, Electric Blue, Deep Rose, Burnt Orange, etc.).\n   188\t* **Override:** if the brand or brief explicitly asks for purple / violet / lila, embrace it. But execute with intent: consistent palette, harmonised neutrals, restrained gradients. Not generic AI gradient slop.\n   189\t* **One palette per project.** Do not fluctuate between warm and cool grays within the same project.\n   190\t* **COLOR CONSISTENCY LOCK (mandatory):** Once an accent color is chosen for a page, it is used on the WHOLE page. DIAL DEFINITIONS (Technical Reference)\\n\\n### DESIGN_VARIANCE (Level 1-10)\\n* **1-3 (Predictable):** Symmetrical CSS Grid (12-col, equal fr-units), equal paddings, centered alignment.\\n* **4-7 (Offset):** `margin-top: -2rem` overlaps, varied image aspect ratios (4:3 next to 16:9), left-aligned headers over center-aligned data.\\n* **8-10 (Asymmetric):** Masonry layouts, CSS Grid with fractional units (`grid-template-columns: 2fr 1fr 1fr`), massive empty zones (`padding-left: 20vw`).\\n* **MOBILE OVERRIDE:** For levels 4-10, asymmetric layouts above `md:` MUST collapse to strict single-column (`w-full`, `px-4`, `py-8`) on viewports `< 768px`.\\n\\n### MOTION_INTENSITY (Level 1-10)\\n* **1-3 (Static):** No automatic animations. Break the pattern with a full-width section, a vertical-stack section, a bento grid, a marquee, or a different layout family.\\n* **EYEBROW RESTRAINT (mandatory, the #1 violated rule in production tests).** An \\\"eyebrow\\\" is the small uppercase wide-tracking label sitting above a section headline (e.g. `FOUR COLORWAYS`, `SELECTED WORK`, `THE HARDWARE`, `Git-native task management`). Typical CSS signature: `text-[11px] uppercase tracking-[0.18em]`, `font-mono text-[10.5px] uppercase tracking-[0.22em]`. Every AI-built site puts an eyebrow above EVERY section header, producing the same templated rhythm. Hard rule:\\n  - **Maximum 1 eyebrow per 3 sections.** Hero counts as 1. So a page with 9 sections may use at most 3 eyebrows total.\\n  - If section A has an eyebrow, the next 2 sections cannot have one.\\n  - **Pre-Flight Check is mechanical:** count instances of `uppercase tracking` (or similar small-caps mono labels above headlines) across all section components. If count > ceil(sectionCount / 3), the output fails.\\n  - **What to do instead of an eyebrow:** drop it entirely. The headline alone is enough. If you need to categorize a section, the section's location on the page already categorizes it; no label needed.\\n* **SPLIT-HEADER BAN (mandatory).** The pattern \\\"left big headline + right small explainer paragraph\\\" as a section header (left col-span-7/8, right col-span-4/5 with a small body paragraph floating in the right column) is **banned as default**. Sections should have ONE focused message. If you genuinely need both a headline and an explainer paragraph, stack them vertically (headline on top, body below, max-width 65ch). Reach for the split-header pattern only when there is a real compositional reason (e.g., the right column carries a visual or interactive element, not just filler text).\\n* **Bento Background Diversity (mandatory).** Bento and feature-grid sections cannot be 6 white-on-white cards with text inside. At least 2-3 cells in any multi-cell grid need real visual variation: a real image, a brand-appropriate gradient (not AI-purple), a pattern, a tinted background. A cream-on-cream bento with only typography inside reads as boring AI default, even when the rest of the page is good.\\n* **Mobile collapse must be explicit per section.** For every multi-column layout, declare the `< 768px` fallback in the same component. No \\\"it'll work, Tailwind handles it\\\" assumptions.\\n\\n### 4.8 Image & Visual Asset Strategy\\n\\nLanding pages and portfolios are **visual products**. Text-only pages with fake-screenshot divs are slop.\\n\\n**Priority order for visual assets:**\\n1. **Image-generation tool first.** If ANY image-gen tool is available in the environment (`generate_image`, MCP image tool, IDE-integrated gen, OpenAI image tools, etc.) you MUST use it to create section-specific assets: hero photography, product shots, texture backgrounds, mood images. Generate at the right aspect ratio for the section. Do not skip this step because hand-rolled CSS feels faster.\\n2. **Real web images second.** When no gen tool is available, use real photography sources. Acceptable defaults:\\n   * `https://picsum.photos/seed/{descriptive-seed}/{w}/{h}` for placeholder photography (seed should describe the section, e.g. `marrow-cookware-kitchen`)\\n   * Actual stock or brand URLs when the brief provides them\\n   * Open-license sources (Unsplash via direct URL, Pexels) if explicitly allowed\\n3. **Last resort: tell the user.** If neither is possible, do NOT fill the page with hand-rolled SVG illustrations or div-based \\\"fake screenshots.\\\" Instead, leave clearly-labeled placeholder slots (`<!-- TODO: hero product photo, 1600x1200 -->`) and at the end of the response say: *\\\"This page needs real images at: \\\\[list of placements\\\\]. Please generate or provide them.\\\"*\\n\\n**Even minimalist sites need real images.** A pure-text page is not minimalism. It is incomplete work. Even an editorial Linear-style site needs at least 2-3 real images (hero, one product/lifestyle shot, one supporting image). Generate B&W minimalist photography if the brief is restrained; do not skip images entirely because the dial is low.\\n\\n**Real company logos for social proof.** When the brief calls for a \\\"Trusted by / Used by / Customers\\\" logo wall, do NOT default to plain text wordmarks (`<span>Acme Co</span>` styled in a row). Use real SVG logos:\\n* **Source: Simple Icons** (`https://cdn.simpleicons.org/{slug}/ffffff` for any color, or `simple-icons` npm package). Covers most known brands.\\n* **Alternative: devicon** for tech-stack logos (`@svgr/cli` or CDN).\\n* **Make-up the brand name? Then make-up an SVG mark too.** Generate a simple monogram (one letter in a circle, two-letter ligature, abstract glyph) rendered as an inline `<svg>` matching the page style. Plain text wordmarks for invented brand names look generic.\\n* **Always** ensure logos render in both light and dark mode (white-on-dark, black-on-light, or single-color theme variable).\\n* **LOGO-ONLY rule (mandatory):** logo wall = logos and nothing else. Do NOT print industry / category labels below each logo (no `Vercel` + `hosting` underneath, no `Stripe` + `payments`, no `Cloudflare` + `infra`). The logo is the credibility, the label adds nothing the user does not already know. Optional: brand name as alt-text for screen readers, optional link to the brand's site. That is it.\\n\\n**Hand-rolled illustrations:**\\n* SVG icons from libraries: fine (see Section 3.C).\\n* Hand-rolled decorative SVGs (custom illustrations, logos, marks): **strongly discouraged**, never as default. Acceptable only when:\\n  - The brief explicitly calls for it (\\\"draw me an SVG logo\\\")\\n  - It's a single, simple geometric mark (a square, a circle, a wordmark in display type)\\n  - You're confident in the output quality\\n\\n**Div-based fake screenshots are banned.** A \\\"hand-built product preview\\\" rendered with `<div>` rectangles, fake task lists, fake dashboards, fake terminal windows is a Tell. If you need to show a product:\\n* Use a real screenshot URL if one exists\\n* Generate one via image tool\\n* Use a real component preview (an actual mini-version of the UI inside the page)\\n* Or skip the preview entirely and use editorial photography\\n\\n**Hero needs a real visual.** Text + gradient blob is not a hero - it's a placeholder.\\n\\n### 4.9 Content Density\\n\\nLanding pages live on the **first impression**, not the full read. Cut ruthlessly.\\n\\n* **Default content shape per section:** short headline (\\u2264 8 words) + short sub-paragraph (\\u2264 25 words) + one visual asset OR one CTA. Anything more must be justified by the section's job.\\n* **No data-dump sections.** A 20-row publication table, a 30-row award list, a giant pricing matrix on a marketing page = wrong layout. Use:\\n  - Top 3-5 highlights + \\\"View full list\\\" link\\n  - Marquee / carousel for breadth\\n  - Different page entirely if the data is the product\\n* **Long lists need a different UI component, not a longer list.** Default `<ul>` with bullets / `divide-y` rows is the lazy choice. If you have > 5 items, reach for one of these instead:\\n  - 2-column split with grouped items\\n  - Card grid with image + label per item\\n  - Tabs / accordion if items are categorisable\\n  - Horizontal scroll-snap pills\\n  - Carousel for breadth-heavy lists (testimonials, logos, capabilities)\\n  - Marquee for \\\"lots-of-things-that-don't-need-individual-attention\\\"\\n  A spec sheet with 10 rows + a hairline under every row is the WORST default. Either group rows into 2-3 chunks with sparse dividers, or move to a card-per-spec layout.\\n* **Spec sheets specifically (the Marrow-cookware pattern).** A long product specification table with `border-b` on every row is the AI default for cookware / hardware / apparel / artisan-goods briefs. Banned. Concrete alternatives:\\n  - **2-col card grid:** each spec gets its own card with the spec name, the value (large display number), and a one-line \\\"why it matters\\\" body. Cards arranged 2-col on desktop, 1-col mobile.\\n  - **Scroll-snap horizontal pills:** each spec is a pill, user can flick through.\\n  - **Grouped chunks:** group 10 specs into 3 logical clusters (e.g. \\\"Materials\\\", \\\"Cooking\\\", \\\"Warranty\\\"), each cluster gets ONE soft divider and a cluster heading.\\n  - **Featured-vs-rest:** 3-4 hero specs visualised as large display tiles, the rest collapsed under a \\\"View full specifications\\\" disclosure.\\n\\n* **COPY SELF-AUDIT (mandatory before ship):** Before declaring any task done, re-read every visible string on the page (headlines, subheads, eyebrows, button labels, body copy, captions, alt text, footer text, error messages). Flag any string that is:\\n  - **Grammatically broken** (\\\"free on its past\\\", \\\"two plans but one is honest\\\", \\\"to put it on the table\\\" out of context)\\n< truncated lines 323-428 >\\n```tsx\\n\\\"use client\\\";\\nimport { useRef, useEffect } from \\\"react\\\";\\nimport { gsap } from \\\"gsap\\\";\\nimport { ScrollTrigger } from \\\"gsap/ScrollTrigger\\\";\\nimport { useReducedMotion } from \\\"motion/react\\\";\\n\\ngsap.registerPlugin(ScrollTrigger);\\n\\nexport function HorizontalPan({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {\\n  const wrap = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);\\n  const track = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);\\n  const reduce = useReducedMotion();\\n\\n  useEffect(() => {\\n    if (reduce || !wrap.current || !track.current) return;\\n    const ctx = gsap.context(() => {\\n      const distance = track.current!.scrollWidth - window.innerWidth;\\n      gsap.to(track.current, {\\n        x: -distance,\\n        ease: \\\"none\\\",\\n        scrollTrigger: {\\n          trigger: wrap.current,\\n          start: \\\"top top\\\",                              // pin starts when section top hits viewport top\\n          end: () => `+=${distance}`,                    // scroll distance = track width minus viewport\\n          pin: true,\\n          scrub: 1,\\n          invalidateOnRefresh: true,\\n        },\\n      });\\n    }, wrap);\\n    return () => ctx.revert();\\n  }, [reduce]);\\n\\n  return (\\n    <section ref={wrap} className=\\\"relative overflow-hidden\\\">\\n      <div ref={track} className=\\\"flex h-[100dvh] items-center\\\">\\n        {children}\\n      </div>\\n    </section>\\n  );\\n}\\n```\\n\\nCritical points: `start: \\\"top top\\\"`, `pin: true`, `end: \\\"+=${distance}\\\"` (scroll length = horizontal travel needed), `scrub: 1`. The wrapper is pinned, the inner track slides horizontally as the user scrolls vertically.\\n\\n### 5.C Scroll-Reveal Stagger - Canonical Skeleton (lighter alternative)\\n\\nFor simple \\\"items appear as they enter viewport\\\" (no pinning), prefer Motion's `whileInView` over GSAP - lighter, no ScrollTrigger needed:\\n\\n```tsx\\n\\\"use client\\\";\\nimport { motion, useReducedMotion } from \\\"motion/react\\\";\\n\\nexport function RevealStagger({ items }: { items: string[] }) {\\n  const reduce = useReducedMotion();\\n  return (\\n    <ul className=\\\"grid gap-6\\\">\\n      {items.map((item, i) => (\\n        <motion.li\\n          key={item}\\n          initial={reduce ? false : { opacity: 0, y: 24 }}\\n          whileInView={{ opacity: 1, y: 0 }}\\n          viewport={{ once: true, amount: 0.3 }}\\n          transition={{\\n            duration: 0.6,\\n            delay: i * 0.06,\\n            ease: [0.16, 1, 0.3, 1],\\n          }}\\n        >\\n          {item}\\n        </motion.li>\\n      ))}\\n    </ul>\\n  );\\n}\\n```\\n\\nUse this for: feature lists, testimonial grids, logo walls, anything that just needs \\\"enter on scroll.\\\" Save GSAP for actual pin/scrub work.\\n\\n### 5.D Forbidden Animation Patterns\\n\\n* **`window.addEventListener(\\\"scroll\\\", ...)`** is banned. It runs on every scroll frame, jank-prone, no batching. Use Motion's `useScroll()`, GSAP's `ScrollTrigger`, IntersectionObserver, or CSS `scroll-driven animations` (`animation-timeline: view()`).\\n* **Custom scroll progress calculations using `window.scrollY`** in React state. Same reason. Re-renders on every frame.\\n* **`requestAnimationFrame` loops that touch React state.** Use motion values (`useMotionValue` + `useTransform`) instead.\\n* **Layout Transitions:** Use Motion's `layout` and `layoutId` props for visible state changes (re-ordering lists, expanding modals, shared elements between routes). Do not wrap static content in `layout` props \\\"for safety\\\" - it costs measurement work.\\n* **Staggered Orchestration:** Use `staggerChildren` (Motion) or CSS cascade (`animation-delay: calc(var(--index) * 100ms)`) for reveal moments where sequence matters. Until you recalculate, every\n    33\tformula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values \u2014 `pandas`,\n    34\t`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.\n    35\t\n    36\t```bash\n    37\tpython scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30\n    38\t```\n    39\t\n    40\tLibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:\n    41\t`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an\n    42\t`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it\n    43\twithheld \u2014 trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it\n    44\tagain. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and\n    45\tonly that case exits non-zero \u2014 `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean\n    46\tworkbook.\n    47\t\n    48\t**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one\n    49\trange or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.\n    50\tWrite 2\u20133 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.\n    51\t\n    52\t**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and\n    53\tthen recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` \u2014 the `[1]` is an index\n    54\tinto the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.\n    55\tThat file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its\n    56\tdata. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for\n    57\treal, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state\n    58\t\u2014 copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,\n    59\tand accepts the loss).\n    60\t\n    61\t## Choosing formulas that survive verification\n    62\t\n    63\tLibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a\n    64\tliteral `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.\n    65\t\n    66\t- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** \u2014 `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` \u2014 which need no prefix.\n    67\t- **Six post-2007 functions work, but only with an `_xlfn.` prefix**, because openpyxl writes your formula into the XML verbatim and Excel stores post-2007 names prefixed (its UI hides the prefix): `_xlfn.TEXTJOIN`, `_xlfn.CONCAT`, `_xlfn.IFS`, `_xlfn.SWITCH`, `_xlfn.MAXIFS`, `_xlfn.MINIFS`. Written bare, each yields `#NAME?`.\n    68\t- **Never use `XLOOKUP`, `XMATCH`, `SORT`, `FILTER`, `UNIQUE`, or `SEQUENCE`.** The runtime's LibreOffice cannot evaluate them under *any* prefix. Newer builds do evaluate them, but they are spilling array functions and an openpyxl-written file has no spill metadata, so only the top-left cell of the range gets a value \u2014 and `recalc.py` reports `total_errors: 0` on the truncated result. Use `INDEX`/`MATCH` for lookups, and sort, filter, and de-duplicate in Python before writing the cells.\n    69\t- A formula LibreOffice could not parse is written back **lowercased** \u2014 a quick tell beside a `#NAME?`.\n    70\t\n    71\t## openpyxl gotchas\n    72\t\n    73\t- **Reading a model takes two loads.** `data_only=True` yields cached values with the formulas gone; the default yields formula strings with no values. One pass cannot give you both.\n    74\t- **`data_only=True` is destructive if you save.** That workbook has no formulas left, so saving replaces every one with a literal \u2014 permanently.\n    75\t- **`data_only=True` on a file openpyxl just wrote returns `None` everywhere** \u2014 run `recalc.py` first. (A formula whose result is `\"\"` also reads back as `None`.)\n    76\t- **Merged cells: write the top-left anchor only.** Every other cell in the range is a `MergedCell` whose `.value` is read-only.\n    77\t- **`.xlsm` loses its macros unless you pass `keep_vba=True`** to `load_workbook`.\n    78\t- **A sheet name containing a space must be quoted** in a cross-sheet reference: `='Assumptions Inputs'!$B$5`. Unquoted, it evaluates to `#VALUE!`.\n    79\t\n    80\t## Financial models\n    81\t\n    82\tUnless the user says otherwise, or the existing file already does something else.\n    83\t\n    84\t**Color:** blue text (`0,0,255`) for hardcoded inputs and scenario levers \u00b7 black for formulas \u00b7\n    85\tgreen (`0,128,0`) for links to another sheet \u00b7 red (`255,0,0`) for links to another file \u00b7\n    86\tyellow fill (`255,255,0`) for key assumptions and cells the user should fill in.\n    87\t\n    88\t**Numbers:** currency `$#,##0`, with the unit named in the header (`Revenue ($mm)`) \u00b7 zeros\n    89\trender as `-`, including in percentages (`$#,##0;($#,##0);-`) \u00b7 negatives in parentheses \u00b7\n    90\tpercentages `0.0%`, **stored as fractions** (`0.15` renders `15.0%`; storing `15` renders\n    91\t`1500.0%`) \u00b7 valuation multiples `0.0x` \u00b7 years as text (`\"2024\"`, never `2,024`).\n    92\t\n    93\t**Structure:** every assumption in its own labeled cell, referenced by the formulas that use it\n    94\t(`=B5*(1+$B$6)`, never `=B5*1.05`) \u00b7 formulas consistent across every projection period, since a\n    95\tlone edited cell mid-row is the commonest silent error \u00b7 guard denominators that can be zero.\n    96\t\n    97\t## Dependencies\n    98\t\n    99\t`openpyxl`, `pandas`, `markitdown` (pip, preinstalled \u2014 install only if an import fails or the command is missing) \u00b7 LibreOffice (`soffice`, auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)\n   100\t"

Its entire reason to exist is to stop you from doing the easy, comfortable thing: agreeing with whatever framing the user walked in with. Left alone, a single model answering a single question tends to validate the premise it was handed. The council structurally prevents that by forcing multiple independent, differently-biased advisors to fight over the evidence before anyone gets a verdict.\n    10\t\n    11\tThe goal is not consensus. The goal is a calibrated recommendation plus one concrete next action, with disagreement left visible rather than smoothed over.\n    12\t\n    13\tNever tell the user \"this is definitely the right decision.\" The honest output is: \"given the available evidence, this is the strongest decision we can justify right now \u2014 here is what could make us wrong, and here is the cheapest way to find out.\"\n    14\t\n    15\t## When this triggers\n    16\t\n    17\t- \"council this [decision]\"\n    18\t- \"run this through the council\"\n    19\t- \"council this in red-team mode\"\n    20\t- \"council review\" (post-mortem on a past decision \u2014 see Post-Mortem section below)\n    21\t- Any explicit request for an adversarial / multi-perspective review of a decision\n    22\t\n    23\tWhen triggered, do not answer the user's question directly. Trigger whenever the user says \\\\\\\"council this,\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\"run this through the council,\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\"council review,\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\"council this in red-team mode,\\\\\\\" or explicitly asks for a decision council / adversarial review of a choice. Also offer it proactively when a user is asking you to validate a big, irreversible, or emotionally-loaded decision (launching a product, quitting a job, raising money, a major purchase, a strategic pivot, a hire/fire call) and seems to want reassurance more than analysis. Do not use for small reversible choices or routine questions.\\\"\\n---\\n\\n\\n# Decision Council\\n\\nAn adversarial decision-making workflow. Its entire reason to exist is to stop you from doing the easy, comfortable thing: agreeing with whatever framing the user walked in with. Left alone, a single model answering a single question tends to validate the premise it was handed. The council structurally prevents that by forcing multiple independent, differently-biased advisors to fight over the evidence before anyone gets a verdict.\\n\\nThe goal is not consensus. The goal is a calibrated recommendation plus one concrete next action, with disagreement left visible rather than smoothed over.\\n\\nNever tell the user \\\"this is definitely the right decision.\\\" The honest output is: \\\"given the available evidence, this is the strongest decision we can justify right now \\u2014 here is what could make us wrong, and here is the cheapest way to find out.\\\"\\n\\n## When this triggers\\n\\n- \\\"council this [decision]\\\"\\n- \\\"run this through the council\\\"\\n- \\\"council this in red-team mode\\\"\\n- \\\"council review\\\" (post-mortem on a past decision \\u2014 see Post-Mortem section below)\\n- Any explicit request for an adversarial / multi-perspective review of a decision\\n\\nWhen triggered, do not answer the user's question directly. Run the full workflow below. If you just answer normally, you've defeated the point of invoking this at all.\\n\\nIf the user is asking a normal question, just answer it \\u2014 don't force every decision through five subagents; that's how a useful tool becomes an annoying one.\\n\\n## Pick a mode\\n\\n- **QUICK** \\u2014 3 advisors (Contrarian, First Principles Thinker, Executor), no evidence auditor, no peer review, straight to a lightweight Chairman verdict. Use for low-stakes, easily-reversible decisions.\\n- **STANDARD** (default) \\u2014 5 advisors + Evidence Auditor + anonymous peer review + Challenge Round + Chairman.\\n- **DEEP** \\u2014 5\\u20137 specialized advisors + Evidence Auditor with external verification (when tools allow) + peer review + Challenge Round + Chairman. Use for expensive, irreversible, or strategically important decisions.\\n\\nHonor an explicit mode request (\\\"quick council this,\\\" \\\"deep council this\\\"). Otherwise infer from stakes and reversibility. If it's genuinely unclear, proceed in STANDARD rather than blocking on a clarifying question.\\n\\n## The workflow\\n\\n### Phase 0 \\u2014 Decision Context\\n\\nScan whatever's actually available and relevant (project docs, memory/context, prior decision records, specs, research, financial or customer data, code) for facts bearing on *this specific decision*. Don't dump everything you find into the advisors \\u2014 build a concise Decision Context, and tag every line as workspace/user-sourced fact or your own assumption. Never blur the two.\\n\\n```\\nDECISION CONTEXT\\nWhat is being decided:\\nCurrent situation:\\nKnown facts: [tag each as SOURCED or ASSUMPTION]\\nRelevant constraints:\\nAvailable evidence:\\nImportant unknowns:\\nTime horizon:\\nStakes:\\n```\\n\\n### Phase 1 \\u2014 Neutralize the framing\\n\\nRewrite the user's question so it can't be answered by simply agreeing with them.\\n\\nExample \\u2014 user asks \\\"Should I launch my AI real-estate toolkit?\\\" Bad: repeating that question verbatim. Good: \\\"Given the current product, target customer, evidence of demand, competitive environment, available resources, and opportunity cost, under what conditions would launching now be rational, premature, or irrational?\\\"\\n\\nThen write out explicitly:\\n```\\nDecision: [the actual choice being made]\\nAlternatives: [realistic options beyond yes/no \\u2014 typically: proceed now,\\n  delay and validate, change positioning/scope, reduce scope, abandon,\\n  pursue a different opportunity entirely]\\nObjective: [what outcome actually matters]\\nConstraints: [what can't easily be changed]\\nStakes: [what happens if this decision is wrong]\\nReversibility: [reversible / difficult to reverse / irreversible]\\nTime horizon: [what happens over 1 week / 1 month / 6 months / 1 year]\\n```\\n\\n### Phase 2 \\u2014 Assemble the council\\n\\nDefault roster (five generalists, use unless a domain roster below clearly fits better):\\n\\n1. **The Contrarian** \\u2014 finds reasons the decision could fail: hidden risks, weak assumptions, failure modes, confirmation bias, wishful thinking, opportunity cost. Instruction: assume the user's preferred conclusion is wrong and try to prove it wrong. Only attack claims that matter \\u2014 contrarianism for its own sake is noise.\\n\\n2. **The First Principles Thinker** \\u2014 checks whether this is even the right problem. Asks what's actually true, which assumptions are just inherited convention, what would still be true with every assumption stripped away, and whether a simpler solution exists. Rebuilds the reasoning from fundamental constraints rather than accepting the original framing.\\n\\n3. **The Expansionist** \\u2014 finds upside, asymmetric opportunity, and second-order effects others miss. Assumes the decision could work much better than expected and figures out why. Not blind optimism: every upside claim must name the specific assumption it depends on.\\n\\n4. **The Outsider** \\u2014 reasons with minimal emotional or contextual attachment, explicitly avoiding sunk-cost and insider bias. Give this advisor only the neutral Decision Context, not the full backstory. Prompt: \\\"If you encountered this situation for the first time, with no history and no stake in it, what would you think?\\\" Exists to catch the curse of knowledge.\\n\\n5. **The Executor** \\u2014 turns reasoning into action: feasibility, resources, time, sequencing, what can be tested cheaply this week. Prompt: \\\"What should this person actually do Monday morning?\\\" Must prefer a small reversible experiment over a large irreversible commitment when uncertainty is high.\\n\\n**Adaptive specialists** \\u2014 swap in when the decision clearly sits in a domain, to maximize genuine disagreement rather than running five variations of the same voice:\\n- *Business*: Customer, Market Analyst, Unit Economics, Growth, Operator\\n- *Product*: Customer, Product Strategist, UX, Market, Growth\\n- *Technical*: Architect, Security, Performance, Simplicity, Maintainer\\n- *Financial*: Risk Analyst, Downside Specialist, Opportunity Analyst, Long-Term Investor, Executor\\n- *Career*: Recruiter, Hiring Manager, Industry Insider, Long-Term Strategist, Executor\\n\\nIf nothing fits cleanly, default to the five generalists.\\n\\n### Phase 3 \\u2014 Independent analysis\\n\\nSpawn every advisor as a separate subagent, **in parallel, in one message with multiple tool calls** \\u2014 sequential spawning lets later advisors drift toward earlier framing and defeats the independence the whole exercise depends on. No advisor sees another's output. Give each advisor: the Decision Context, the neutral framing, its mission from Phase 2, and this required schema:\\n\\n```\\nPOSITION: [what you recommend]\\nREASONING: [why]\\nSTRONGEST ARGUMENT: [your single strongest point]\\nWEAKEST ASSUMPTION: [what could make you wrong]\\nEVIDENCE:\\n  - FACT: [directly supported claims]\\n  - INFERENCE: [reasonable conclusions from facts]\\n  - ASSUMPTION: [taken as given without direct support]\\n  - OPINION: [judgment calls, labeled as such]\\nCOUNTERARGUMENT: [the strongest case against your own conclusion]\\nMISSING INFORMATION: [what you wish you knew]\\nFALSIFICATION CONDITION: [what evidence would change your mind]\\nCONFIDENCE: [0-100%, reflecting evidence quality, not writing confidence]\\n```\\n\\nTell each advisor explicitly not to soften its conclusion to be agreeable.\\n\\n### Phase 4 \\u2014 Evidence Auditor\\n\\nA dedicated pass (subagent, or inline for QUICK mode) over every load-bearing claim across all advisors:\\n\\n```\\nCLAIM:\\nCLASSIFICATION: Fact / Inference / Assumption / Opinion\\nEVIDENCE: [what supports it]\\nEVIDENCE QUALITY: Strong / Moderate / Weak / Unsupported\\nCONTRADICTION: [does another advisor's evidence conflict?]\\nFALSIFICATION: [what would prove this wrong]\\n```\\n\\n< truncated lines 130-162 >\\n\\n```\\n1.         "text": "     1\t---\n     2\tname: frontend-design\n     3\tdescription: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.\n     4\tlicense: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt\n     5\t---\n     6\t\n     7\t# Frontend Design\n     8\t\n     9\tApproach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt clich\u00e9 or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.\n    10\t\n    11\t## Ground your designs in the subject matter\n    12\t\n    13\tIf the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from \u2014 a design for a toy for girls aged 8\u201311 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.\n    14\t\n    15\t## Design principles\n    16\t\n    17\tFor web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.\n    18\t\n    19\tTypography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.\n    20\t\n    21\tChoose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.\n    22\t\n    23\tDefault to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.\n    24\t\n    25\tAvoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:\n    26\t- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.\n    27\t- Using all caps for labels.\n    28\t- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.\n    29\t\n    30\tVisual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence \u2014 like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.\n    31\t\n    32\tUse non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment \u2014 one page-load sequence or one reveal \u2014 lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.\n    33\t\n    34\tConsider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.\\nlicense: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt\\n---\\n\\n# Frontend Design\\n\\nApproach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt clich\\u00e9 or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.\\n\\n## Ground your designs in the subject matter\\n\\nIf the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from \\u2014 a design for a toy for girls aged 8\\u201311 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.\\n\\n## Design principles\\n\\nFor web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.\\n\\nTypography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.\\n\\nChoose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.\\n\\nDefault to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.\\n\\nAvoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:\\n- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.\\n- Using all caps for labels.\\n- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.\\n\\nVisual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence \\u2014 like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.\\n\\nUse non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment \\u2014 one page-load sequence or one reveal \\u2014 lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.\\n\\nConsider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.\\n\\n## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique\\n\\nFor calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:\\n1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 \\u2014 Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);\\n2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;\\n3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;\\n4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;\\n5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A \\u00b7 B \\u00b7 C'); labels built as 'WORD \\u2014 fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '\\u2192' appended to link and button text.\\n\\nAll traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly \\u2014 the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.\\n\\nWork in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.\\n- Color: describe the core base palette as 4\\u20136 named hex values.\\n- Type: the typefaces and their roles.\\n- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare.
